newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-REVIEW OF EXPECTATIONS - Australian wages.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-REVIEW OF EXPECTATIONS - Australian wages.

text.p: Australian wages data for the three months to November will be released at 11.30 a.m. (0030 GMT) today.
Wages are a key factor influencing the underlying rate of inflation, and so the outcome will have an impact on interest rate expectations.

The median forecast of the 30 economists surveyed by Reuters is for average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) to have risen 0.9 percent in the quarter, to be 3.6 percent higher over the past year.
Quarterly forecasts ranged from rises of 0.6 to 1.2 percent, leading to annual forecasts between 3.3 and 3.9 percent.
Recent AWOTE data, and forecasts, are detailed below.

Economists tend to pay more attention to the annual rate, which if forecasts are met will have moderated in each of the last five quarters, from a peak of 5.2 percent in August 1995, to be at its lowest level since August 1994.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has said AWOTE is the best wages measure, despite some shortcomings, such as the redefinition of ordinary time hours in enterprise agreements.

"Despite its imperfections, the Bank uses this (AWOTE) as the best single measure of past general wage developments, although the other series are monitored closely as well," the RBA said in its December bulletin.

Wages are a key influence on the underlying rate, and are seen as a important to determining rate expectations because they are a forward looking influence of inflation, and will help shape expectations of what inflation will do in 1997.
In contrast, last week's Decmber quarter inflation confirmed what many had expected -- that inflation had continued to moderate into the end of 1996.

If expectations for Thursday's data are realised, it would suggest the pre-conditions for a rate cut have been met -- low inflation and moderating wages pressures against a backdrop of a still sluggish economy.
However, economists still put the chance of a February rate cut at less than 50 percent. The chances of a rate cut lift after February, and there are a number of reasons for this.
Firstly, some of the weakness in recent data would have already been already been allowed for in the three easings the RBA made in the second half of last year.
Secondly, economists expect the RBA wait on the outcome of the Australian Council of Trade Unions' (ACTU) "living wage" claim, due by early March.
The claim proposes low paid workers recieve an 8.75 percent wage increase in award rates and three A$20 a week 'safety net' increases' over three years.
In December the RBA said "the full living wage claim would imply a mark acceleration of wages growth", estimating it would increase the wages bill by close to two percentage points.

"This direct, alone, would take aggregate growth to well over five percent," the RBA said, adding that flow on effecrts of the claim to other wage claims would mean the full impact of the living wage would be considerably higher.
Last year, former RBA Governor Bernie Fraser had said total employment costs should not exceed 4.5 percent to be consistent with the RBA's underlying inflation target.
The RBA aims to keep the underlying rate to an average of between two to three percent over a run of years.
